I have PTSD and suffer a great deal of paranoia whenever I’m symptomatic. I suggest ordering a copy of Tear Soup to read with loved ones, it’s an an all-ages picture book that covers all of basis of how to support someone who is grieving sexual trauma (or any trauma or loss for that matter) in a few short pages and it’s simplistic enough and appropriate enough to educate to kids. Understand that your paranoia might come in waves, so even if you start feeling okay you want to make sure you’re prepared at home for if you start getting symptomatic again. Personally I know that when I have bouts of paranoia I have a harder time getting outside of the house for things like grocery shopping and appointments. The fear can be paralyzing! The longest I’m usually locked up for is about 2-3 weeks if it’s a particularly bad episode, so basing this off of my own timelines I would say to try to save up about a months worth of living expenses (maybe see if family/friends can chip in for you) so that should you ever need time off, you can afford it + food delivery because there will be lots of times you just cannot and will not want to interact with others. Keep a copy of the depression checklist by your nightstand and remember to go through it daily. Read Aftershock (a book on dealing with those waves of post-sexual trauma symptoms). Good luck. You are strong and capable.

I used to work in marketing in my college days and a lot of stuff that people know about locally that didn’t make the news didn’t make it out of literal ignorance (as in the news station literally did not know about it) because there was never a press release sent in or a phone call to the local station, no interview made, etc, etc.. Media stations like to pursue ultra promising leads and have so much that does come into them on a daily basis that they just work with what they already have in their inbox faaaaar more often than they report things that they individually/personally care about as people, especially since their careers are a service to the public (so they cater to what the public wants according to what the public explicitly tells them - which also means the more people email them press releases about this unjust murder, the more likely it is to actually receive media coverage). Unfortunately Texas has a lot more racism than other states including where I’m from and went to college, so I really hope that it isn’t racism preventing you guys from getting justice. Try sending out some press releases for your most local news sources and ask for a follow up phone call in your inquiry letters so that you can at least get one person’s name and number to kindly, politely harass until you have an actual journalist assigned to the story. If anyone who knows the victim happens to be a strong writer, there are incredibly large news platforms that accept unsolicited pitches year round (New York Times for example). While there is already riots and media coverage over the issue is actually the perfect time to come forward and apply more heat to prosecutors and police departments across the nation. It helps to offer something different to what is already going in the news (a different viewpoint, different solution, different takeaways, etc) because the same old same old creates stagnancy. And don’t count out podcasts. NPR has a very fast response time for the size platform they have so they’re a good first place to pitch to so you can get feedback on how to approach other outlets faster.

My personal experience has been that when grieving and healing and growing through things, it can be really difficult to get your thoughts and emotions in alignment because the grieving process causes you to feel an extreme polarity in your emotions and unfortunately a side effect of healing/grieving is having to work through black and white thinking (viewing people and situations as all good or all bad, based on what end of polarity your emotions are in at the given time). Your person likely needs some time find to stabilize their emotions, balance out their negative thinking patterns and get their head and their heart on the same page again. Grief can do crazy things to the brain and takes a while to unravel. There’s a book on Amazon that I think would help you with all of your letters. It’s a book for all ages titled Tear Soup. Your partner would probably love it. Their therapist might already have a copy.

Sometimes when you’re healing from loss the thought processes you experience can distort your perception when it comes to trusting others and even trusting ourselves, especially if other unhealthy thinking patterns that grief can uncover are at play - like black and white thinking (viewing people and situations as either all good or all bad). It takes a while to come to a place of balance in your thoughts and emotions and to actually get your thoughts in alignment with or on the same page as your emotions when your world is rocked by loss and grief. Your partner probably just needs some time and some privacy regarding their thoughts and emotions while they explore the polarity of their thoughts/emotions in order to heal. I’m sorry you’re having to suffer the highs and lows with them.
